batch.method: Manual visual correction against rendered PDF pages, using PaddleOCR-VL output only as a scaffold.
policy: Preserve Lovejoy's abbreviations and argumentative structure where readable.
Do not silently normalize difficult ethnographic names, foreign-language titles, or bibliographic references.
Use [illegible]/[?] and confidence flags for uncertain readings.
Where handwriting is too poor for diplomatic transcription, retain only source-supported argumentative structure rather than hallucinating lexical detail.

research_signals_from_batch: PDF p.64 directly distinguishes two modes within magical sacrifice: technically hazardous coercive relation with personal gods and direct action upon natural forces. The component mechanical/magical grammar is Frazer/Marillier-field material; the page-level two-branch redistribution remains locally significant.

PDF p.65 directly says sacrificial forms are commonly mingled and require 'delicate analysis' to dissociate their ritual elements; survivance/syncretism is field-owned, while the explicit analytical dissociation procedure is W3 and locally evidenced.

PDF p.66 directly indexes ritual mechanism to competent/social bearer: expiatory sacrifice is generally performed by the whole community, whereas magical sacrifice is performed by priests possessing magical skill in charms. This remains one of the strongest W3/A2 relation-level seams in 005.

Funerary sacrifice, cannibalism, failed-specialist killing, animal sanctity and provision for the dead belong to a crowded source field; pp.67-72 remain primarily case/mechanism summaries until exact local reclassification wording is recovered.

PDF p.69 directly rejects animal sacrifice as a straightforward sign of advancement and records an animal->human substitution direction. That direction is Robertson-Smith-field material; its use against a universal progress ladder is the safer local significance.

PDF p.73 directly preserves 'another meaning' in a funerary-practice reinterpretation sequence. Tylor owns object-soul/destruction-as-release and Marillier owns the survivance problem; the local page operation is explanatory reassignment among available interpretations.

Across pp.61-75, the defensible Lovejoy-local residue lies in relations among mechanism, performer/jurisdiction, case allocation and historical explanation rather than ownership of the component ritual categories.

pages.corrected_text:
No. 18. The page describes magical sacrifice as 'a sort of machine' which one should not put into operation unless one is sure of remaining master of it: 'the gods will take advantage of a man's lack of technical skill with the magical apparatus to subject him in turn to their will.' The immediately following characterization of the transaction between god and sacrificer remains partly compressed/uncertain.

The notes then distinguish magical sacrifices that do not work by constraint upon the will of gods but directly upon forces of nature; an imitative rain-producing act is used as an example of efficacy through a supposed unity/link in nature.

pages.corrected_text:
[Continuation.] The page says sacrificial forms are not, in the majority of cases, sharply marked off from one another or found separately with each idea in its purity. Far more commonly two or more are mingled, so that only by a 'delicate analysis' can one dissociate the different ritual elements. It adds that fusion / syncretism has often been preceded by a period in which the several sacrifices were distinct in character and function; later they become combined.

A following source-rich cluster concerns offerings to the dead: food, blood, libations and human victims can appear within funerary/provision practices whose underlying ideas are various and mixed.

[Funerary sacrifice.] Provision for the dead is described through continuation of possessions/service into the future life, including killing attendants/slaves around high-status dead.

On the facing page the image-secure core distinguishes performance by sacrificial type. Expiatory sacrifice is 'very generally performed' by the whole community, which thereby disembarrasses itself of responsibility for the crime/offence [middle clause partly compressed]. Magical sacrifice, by contrast in ritual organization, is performed by priests, specifically those possessing magical skill in charms. The page therefore relates ritual type to a distinct social bearer or competent agent.

pages.corrected_text:
The page continues a discussion of religious elements under changing social conditions and then directly rejects a simple evolutionary reading of victim type: 'animal' sacrifice is 'not an evidence of advancement'; it says animal sacrifice is commonly more primitive than human sacrifice, dating from a period of extreme respect for a particular animal, 'for whom t. hum. victim [has] been substituted.' The final verb/auxiliary is slightly compressed, but the animal -> human substitution direction is clear.

The historical direction itself is available in the Robertson-Smith sacrifice field. The page remains valuable as an image-secure use of that counter-arrow against victim species as a universal progress index, not as evidence that Lovejoy originated the substitution direction.

pages.corrected_text: Burning/destruction at funerals is treated as a case of explanatory reinterpretation. The page first records a practice connected with protecting the living against return of the dead, comparing it with placing a heavy stone on a tomb. It then says the practice can develop 'another meaning', based on the idea that the spirit is not properly released unless the body is completely destroyed; burning becomes the evident means. On the facing page, breaking/smashing objects placed with the dead is compared with releasing the object's soul/spirit so the dead may use it in the other world.
